review.title: Nhận xét bài viết trên lớp
paragraphs: Some people argue that schools should give rewards to students with the highest academic achievements, whereas others believe that recognising student's progress is more important. Personally, I believe that schools should reward both.

Admittedly, rewarding students with the best academic results is true. Initially, students who have diligently applied themselves to their studies, leading to they receiving their praises and privileges. This may encourage those students and others to study harder to win the rewards, which can propel towards overall academic gains. Furthermore, this kind of competition can be seen in almost every aspect of life, where only the best individuals are rewarded. Students are used to this reality and thrive in the face of fierce competition, enabling them to achieve success in later life.

However, students who show improvement should also reward. Only a few smart students can come first and receive the rewards, causing others to think that their effort is futile because they can not surpass those outstanding individuals. As a result, they are feeling overwhelmed and disheartened which can gradually lose the incentive to study. In addition, emphasizing improvements can encourage all students to understand be diligent in their studies and help students to understand that they need to constantly improve themselves and irrespective of how well they have been or are performing. The constant desire to outdo themselves can even benefit themselves more than the competitive determination to win against all others.
In conclusion, I am firmly convinced that schools should be rewarded for both groups, including students with the best academic result and students who show improvement.

paragraphs: Nowadays, some people argue that public museums and art galleries may become unnecessary as people can view historical objects and works of art on a computer. Personally, I am of the opposite school of thought.

Admittedly, technology brings significant benefits to people seeking cultural and historical resources. High-resolution images, three-dimensional reconstructions; virtual reality platforms enable viewers to explore masterpieces and ancient artefacts in remarkable detail without leaving home. For instance, the Louvre museum provides many items from its collection on online platforms, allowing people who cannot afford to travel or have mobility issues to still access a vast range of cultural and historical heritages.

However, I strongly believe that public museums and art galleries are still essential. Initially, the online experience cannot replicate the direct sensory engagement of seeing an artefact or artwork in person. Seeing such objects in person may evoke emotions and a sense of authenticity that digital images cannot convey. For example, visitors can see historical objects and artworks in galleries up close, appreciate their details and feel more connected to the past. Furthermore, museums and galleries are vital cultural hubs that symbolize the identity of a region. This cultural role can attract tourists and foster bonding within the community.
In conclusion, in light of these arguments, I strongly challenge the perspective that public museums and art galleries will become unnecessary.

paragraphs: It is often debated whether children should learn through trial and error or adults should help them avoid mistakes. Personally, I am of the former school of thought: children should be allowed to learn from failures, provided that the errors do not involve serious danger.

On the one hand, those who want adults to prevent mistakes have several reasons. Initially, many mistakes are avoidable: children do not need to be hurt by knives, fire or electricity to learn to be careful. Furthermore, shielding children from harm is a fundamental parental duty, and forestalling such mistakes helps parents fulfil it. Finally, pre-emptively helping children gives parents peace of mind since they know they are doing their best to protect and raise them.

On the other hand, supporters of letting children learn from mistakes have their own valid reasoning. To begin with, it is practically impossible to prevent all mistakes since parents cannot be around all the time. As children experiment with new things, some mistakes become inevitable. Moreover, through trial and error, children can learn invaluable lessons that will stand them in good stead later in life. More importantly, this helps them avoid overdependence. If they are shielded from everything, they may grow up overdependent on others, an undesirable trait.

In conclusion, while it is important to protect children from serious harm, I believe that experiencing ordinary mistakes is crucial for their development and can help prepare them for the future. Parents must still intervene and give guidance on important matters to prevent errors that may derail their future.

paragraphs: The given bar chart illustrates how much carbon emissions was released from gas, oil and coal in the United kingdom over a 20-year period, commencing 1990.

Overall, there was an increase in the amount of greenhouse gas from burning gas, while the oil and coal witnessed a downward trend. In addition, at the beginning of the period, coal was the largest source of emissions, but it was overtaken by gas, which became the largest contributor by the end of the period.

To elaborate, in 1990, the quantity of carbon emissions from gas started at just over 220 million tons, after which it experienced a steady growth to 270 million tons in 1995. In stark contrast, the amount of greenhouse gas produced from oil was roughly 270 million tons by in the first year, followed by a slight decline to 240 million tons after 5 years. Similarly, the coal emissions experienced the most dramatic fall, plummeting from 310 millions tons in 1990 to become the highest figure at roughly 280 million tons by 1995.

Regarding categories with opposite changes, carbon emissions from gas exhibited a slight growth, climbing from approximately 300 million tons in 2000 to roughly 320 million tons in 2010, making the highest point of entire chart. The figure for oil and coal, conversely, went down by 50 and 60 million tons respectively over the whole timeline.

Em cần kiểm tra lại mốc thời gian của từng phép giảm: 50 và 60 triệu tấn là mức giảm từ năm 2000 đến 2010, không phải toàn giai đoạn. Overall, emissions from gas increased and became the highest of the three by 2000. By contrast, those from coal fell throughout the period. Oil ended lower than it began, although its emissions rose briefly between 1995 and 2000.

In 1990, gas produced about 220 million tons of emissions, compared with around 270 million tons from oil and 310 million tons from coal. Gas then rose to roughly 270 million tons in 1995 and 300 million tons in 2000. Over the same ten years, coal declined to about 250 million tons. Oil fell to 240 million tons in 1995 before recovering to approximately 260 million tons five years later.

From 2000 onwards, gas continued to climb, reaching about 320 million tons in 2010. The other two fuels moved in the opposite direction during this period: oil emissions dropped by around 50 million tons to 210 million tons, while those from coal fell by about 60 million tons to 190 million tons.

paragraphs: The question of whether school curricula should prioritize history or subjects like science and technology is a subject of ongoing debate. Personally, I firmly believe that history or subjects like science and technology are inherently non-comparable because they have the distinct merits of each field.

On the one hand, history is equally crucial as it provides the ethical and cultural framework that guides human progress. Initially, studying history offer some lessons about the past, understand events from multiple perspectives and the evolution of political and social systems. Furthermore This fosters comprehensive thinking, empathy and teaching society. For instance, studying past wars and economic crises can help students have more opportunities to gain an over view of various fields of knowledge and thus understand diverse aspects of life. Therefore, history is not only provide knowledge about the past, but it also helps students develop a deeper understanding of the present.

On the other hand, subjects like science and technology are arguably more relevant to this practical demands of modern life. Scientific disciplines such as technology, math, ... offer students understand the natural phenomena, address some practical problems and apply to both everyday life and future careers. Unlike history, which could help student interpret the past, subjects like science and technology provide them with the tools to shape the future and become a well-rounded person. Therefore, prioritizing these subjects provide knowledge to advance human civilization and sustain economic growth.

In conclusion, while science and technology provide the necessary tools for innovation and economic advancement, history helps the young people understand the past that guides human progress. Therefore, I firmly believe that both disciplines are equally important and must coexist.
review.overall: Cô thấy em đã bàn được cả hai quan điểm và giữ được ý kiến rằng lịch sử cùng khoa học đều cần thiết. paragraphs.text: School subjects are often ranked by their supposed usefulness, with some people favouring history and others giving priority to science and technology. I believe both deserve a place in the curriculum because they prepare students for different aspects of adult life.

History helps young people understand how societies came to be and why present institutions and values matter. By studying a past war, for example, students can consider the decisions that led to conflict and the consequences for ordinary people. This gives them a basis for discussing peace, civic responsibility and competing interpretations of events. Historical study can also build respect for cultural traditions without asking students to accept every past decision uncritically. Such knowledge is useful when they take part in public debates or make choices that affect their communities.

Science and technology, meanwhile, equip students to investigate the natural world and address practical problems. In science lessons, pupils learn to test an explanation against evidence; in technology lessons, they can apply that habit to designing useful tools. For instance, understanding basic biology and digital systems can help them evaluate health information and use new technology responsibly. These subjects also provide foundations for careers in healthcare, engineering and research. Their value therefore extends beyond future employment to informed decisions in everyday life.

In conclusion, history offers insight into human experience, while science and technology develop the ability to investigate and improve the material world. Neither contribution makes the other unnecessary. Schools should teach both and help students connect the lessons they offer.
